items.stem: On which date did the UN estimate that the world population reached 8 billion?
items.answer: 15 November 2022
items.markingKey: 15 November 2022. 7 billion was marked on 31 October 2011.

items.stem: Explain the difference between population density and population distribution.
items.answer: Distribution describes the pattern of where people live; density is a measurement of how many people live per km² in an area.
items.markingKey: Distribution describes the pattern of where people live; density is a measurement of how many people live per km² in an area. One mark for a correct account of each side; further marks for making the difference explicit (not two separate definitions).

items.stem: A student claims: "Large countries always have large populations." Identify the error in this claim and correct it.
items.answer: Area does not decide population: Canada and Australia are huge but have small populations, while Bangladesh is small but has over 170 million people.
items.markingKey: Area does not decide population: Canada and Australia are huge but have small populations, while Bangladesh is small but has over 170 million people. 1 mark for identifying the error, 1-2 marks for the correct explanation.

items.stem: Using accurate subject terminology and at least one specific example, write a structured paragraph that responds to: Explain why the Sahara is sparsely populated.
items.answer: It is extremely hot and dry, with very little rainfall, poor soils and few water sources, so it is hard to grow food or build settlements.
items.markingKey: Content: It is extremely hot and dry, with very little rainfall, poor soils and few water sources, so it is hard to grow food or build settlements. Structure: a clear point that answers the question, specific evidence, explanation that links evidence to the point, and a closing link. Criterion C (communicating): appropriate style and register for the purpose, a clear structure suited to the format (topic sentence, developed evidence, explanation, link back to the question), accurate subject terminology, and sources documented with a recognised convention (MLA or APA).

items.stem:
Using the data below, calculate the population density of Australia.
Population (2023 estimate): 26,600,000
Area: 7,692,024 km²
items.answer: 3.5 people per km²
items.markingKey: Density = population ÷ area (M1) = 26,600,000 ÷ 7,692,024 = 3.5 people per km² (A1). Units required.

items.stem: Describe the research methods you would use to answer "Why is the population of Peru concentrated on its narrow coastal desert rather than in the Amazon region?", naming specific sources and explaining why each is appropriate.
items.answer: Collect INEI census data by region; draw a choropleth map of density; overlay maps of relief, climate and roads; read two secondary sources; explain the pattern; evaluate data reliability.
items.markingKey: Indicative plan: Collect INEI census data by region; draw a choropleth map of density; overlay maps of relief, climate and roads; read two secondary sources; explain the pattern; evaluate data reliability. Credit: logical sequence of steps with a timeline; varied, appropriate sources (primary and secondary) named specifically; a method for recording and citing information (e.g. a source log in MLA/APA); a step for evaluating the process and results. Criterion B (investigating): a clear, focused research question whose relevance is justified, a realistic action plan, appropriate and varied methods/sources, and reflection on the process.

items.stem: Which term matches this description: "A feature created by people, such as jobs, transport, services or government policy, that influences where people live"?
items.answer: human factor
items.markingKey: C. This is the definition of human factor.

items.stem: Explain why many of the world's largest cities are on coasts or rivers.
items.answer: Coasts and rivers provide water, trade and transport routes, fishing and flat land, so ports grew into big cities such as Shanghai, Mumbai and Lagos.
items.markingKey: Award marks for: Coasts and rivers provide water, trade and transport routes, fishing and flat land, so ports grew into big cities such as Shanghai, Mumbai and Lagos. (2 marks: one for each linked point in the chain of reasoning; no marks for assertion without explanation.)

items.stem: "Cold places always have no people." Explain the flaw in this statement.
items.answer: Cold places can be sparsely populated, but people live in them where there are resources, e.g. mining towns in Siberia or Arctic communities.
items.markingKey: Cold places can be sparsely populated, but people live in them where there are resources, e.g. mining towns in Siberia or Arctic communities. 1 mark for identifying the error, 1-2 marks for the correct explanation.

items.stem: Justify the relevance of the research question "Why is the population of Peru concentrated on its narrow coastal desert rather than in the Amazon region?"
items.answer: It investigates physical and human factors in one country, with census data and maps available.
items.markingKey: It investigates physical and human factors in one country, with census data and maps available. Award marks for relevance to the unit's concepts or global context, and for showing the question is focused and can be answered with available sources. Criterion B (investigating): a clear, focused research question whose relevance is justified, a realistic action plan, appropriate and varied methods/sources, and reflection on the process.

items.stem: Which of the following is the most clear and focused research question for an investigation into population distribution and density, and the physical and human factors that affect them?
options: Why are there so many people?
Why is the population of Peru concentrated on its narrow coastal desert rather than in the Amazon region?
items.answer: Why is the population of Peru concentrated on its narrow coastal desert rather than in the Amazon region?
items.markingKey: C. It is open, has a clear scope (place/period/group) and can be answered with evidence; the others are too broad, closed or off-topic.

items.stem:
Source A – UN press release (paraphrased): Summary of the United Nations "World Population Prospects 2022" press release

The world's population reached 8 billion on 15 November 2022. It took 12 years to grow from 7 billion to 8 billion, but it is expected to take about 15 years to reach 9 billion, because growth is slowing. More than half of the increase up to 2050 will be concentrated in just eight countries.

How reliable is Source A for someone researching population distribution and density, and the physical and human factors that affect them? Justify your answer using its origin and purpose.
items.answer: Origin: Summary of the United Nations "World Population Prospects 2022" press release. Purpose: to inform governments and the public about global population trends. Value: The UN is the main global source of population estimates, so the data are authoritative. Limitation: Future figures are projections based on assumptions about birth and death rates and may change.
items.markingKey: Origin: Summary of the United Nations "World Population Prospects 2022" press release. Purpose: to inform governments and the public about global population trends. Value: The UN is the main global source of population estimates, so the data are authoritative. Limitation: Future figures are projections based on assumptions about birth and death rates and may change. Award up to [3]: origin and purpose identified and USED (not just copied), at least one value and one limitation explicitly linked to them. Reliability is judged for a purpose, not as "biased = useless". MYP I&S criterion D (year 3), scaled to the marks: 7-8 thoroughly analyses concepts and issues, summarises information to make valid, well-supported arguments, analyses a range of sources in terms of origin and purpose recognising value and limitations, and clearly recognises different perspectives and their implications; 5-6 substantial; 3-4 adequate, partly descriptive; 1-2 limited, mostly assertion.

items.stem: Plan an extended response to the question: "Physical factors are more important than human factors in explaining population distribution." To what extent do you agree? Give a thesis, two arguments with specific evidence, a counter-argument and a conclusion.
items.answer: Thesis: At the global scale physical factors explain the broad pattern, but at regional and local scales human factors are increasingly decisive.
items.markingKey: Arguments for: climate, water and relief set limits – deserts, ice caps and mountains are sparsely populated; most dense areas are fertile lowlands with water. Counter-arguments: jobs and services in cities draw people regardless of physical conditions, e.g. Dubai; government policy and history shape distribution, e.g. Brasília. Thesis/conclusion: At the global scale physical factors explain the broad pattern, but at regional and local scales human factors are increasingly decisive. Credit a thesis that answers the question, logically ordered paragraphs each with specific evidence, a counter-argument that is weighed, and a conclusion that follows. Criterion C (communicating): appropriate style and register for the purpose, a clear structure suited to the format (topic sentence, developed evidence, explanation, link back to the question), accurate subject terminology, and sources documented with a recognised convention (MLA or APA).

items.stem: Which of the following best describes "settlement hierarchy"?
options: Describes an area with few people per square kilometre
The way people are spread out across an area
The number of live births per 1 000 people per year
The ranking of settlements by size and number of services, from isolated dwelling to megacity
items.answer: The ranking of settlements by size and number of services, from isolated dwelling to megacity
items.markingKey: D. "settlement hierarchy" is the ranking of settlements by size and number of services, from isolated dwelling to megacity.

items.stem: Explain why the situation of Singapore helped it become a major port city.
items.answer: It lies on the Strait of Malacca, one of the world's busiest shipping lanes between the Indian and Pacific Oceans, so ships stop there to trade and refuel.
items.markingKey: Award marks for: It lies on the Strait of Malacca, one of the world's busiest shipping lanes between the Indian and Pacific Oceans, so ships stop there to trade and refuel. (2 marks: one for each linked point in the chain of reasoning; no marks for assertion without explanation.)

items.stem: A student claims: "Larger settlements always have the same functions as smaller ones, only more of them." Identify the error in this claim and correct it.
items.answer: Larger settlements also have higher-order functions not found in small ones, such as universities, airports and specialist hospitals.
items.markingKey: Larger settlements also have higher-order functions not found in small ones, such as universities, airports and specialist hospitals. 1 mark for identifying the error, 1-2 marks for the correct explanation.

items.stem:
Source A – Geography textbook (paraphrased): Paraphrase of a standard explanation of the settlement hierarchy in secondary-school geography textbooks, based on Christaller's central place theory (1933)

Settlements can be arranged in a hierarchy. At the bottom are many small hamlets and villages offering few, low-order services. Towards the top are fewer but larger towns and cities offering many services, including high-order ones such as universities, specialist hospitals and international airports.

Explain one value and one limitation of Source A for an investigation into settlement site, situation and function, and the settlement hierarchy, referring to its origin and purpose.
items.answer: Origin: Paraphrase of a standard explanation of the settlement hierarchy in secondary-school geography textbooks, based on Christaller's central place theory (1933). Purpose: to explain a model to students. Value: It summarises a widely used model clearly. Limitation: Models simplify reality; online shopping and car travel have changed how people use services.

items.stem: Outline one way in which Durham, England shows a defensive site.
items.answer: The cathedral and castle stand on a high peninsula almost surrounded by a meander of the River Wear. The river loop protected the settlement on three sides.
items.markingKey: Context (The cathedral and castle stand on a high peninsula almost surrounded by a meander of the River Wear.) – 1 mark for accurate, specific detail. Link: the river loop protected the settlement on three sides. – remaining marks for explicitly connecting the example to a defensive site.

items.stem: Write the introduction and an outline of the body paragraphs for an essay that evaluates the view that "Situation is more important than site for the growth of a settlement today."
items.answer: Thesis: Situation is usually more important for growth today, while site was more important for a settlement's origin and still affects risk and cost.
items.markingKey: Arguments for: modern cities grow because of connections – transport, trade and links to other places; technology can overcome most site problems. Counter-arguments: site still affects flood risk, water supply and building costs; many historic cities owe their origin to site. Thesis/conclusion: Situation is usually more important for growth today, while site was more important for a settlement's origin and still affects risk and cost. Credit a thesis that answers the question, logically ordered paragraphs each with specific evidence, a counter-argument that is weighed, and a conclusion that follows. Criterion C (communicating): appropriate style and register for the purpose, a clear structure suited to the format (topic sentence, developed evidence, explanation, link back to the question), accurate subject terminology, and sources documented with a recognised convention (MLA or APA).

items.stem: A newsagent is an example of a low-order service because…
options: it is only found in cities
it has a low threshold and short range
items.answer: it has a low threshold and short range
items.markingKey: D. People buy newspapers often and nearby.

items.stem: Explain the difference between threshold and range.
items.answer: Threshold is the minimum number of customers needed for a service to survive; range is the maximum distance people will travel to use it.
items.markingKey: Threshold is the minimum number of customers needed for a service to survive; range is the maximum distance people will travel to use it. One mark for a correct account of each side; further marks for making the difference explicit (not two separate definitions).

items.answer: It also considers the number and range of services and the size of the sphere of influence.
items.markingKey: It also considers the number and range of services and the size of the sphere of influence. 1 mark for identifying the error, 1-2 marks for the correct explanation.

items.answer: Weakness: it asks only for a definition Improved: "How does the number and type of services change with settlement size in the district around our school?"

items.stem: Write one well-structured paragraph (Point, Evidence, Explanation, Link) in answer to this question: Explain why the function of a settlement can change over time.
items.answer: Economic change alters jobs – e.g. a mining town may become a tourist centre when mines close, or a fishing port may become a commuter town.

items.stem: You have three weeks to investigate "How does the number and type of services change with settlement size in the district around our school?" Outline a step-by-step plan, the sources you would use and one way you would evaluate your process at the end.

items.stem: Outline the meaning of the term "birth rate".
items.answer: The number of live births per 1 000 people per year
items.markingKey: 1 mark for the core idea: the number of live births per 1 000 people per year. Award full marks only if the defining feature is clear; a vague example alone scores 0.

items.stem: Briefly explain why a population can keep growing even after fertility falls to replacement level.
items.answer: Population momentum: a large number of young people will still reach child-bearing age, so births exceed deaths for decades.
items.markingKey: Award marks for: Population momentum: a large number of young people will still reach child-bearing age, so births exceed deaths for decades. (2 marks: one for each linked point in the chain of reasoning; no marks for assertion without explanation.)

items.stem: Explain the difference between fertility rate and birth rate.
items.answer: The birth rate is births per 1 000 people in the whole population each year; the fertility rate is the average number of children per woman over her lifetime.
items.markingKey: The birth rate is births per 1 000 people in the whole population each year; the fertility rate is the average number of children per woman over her lifetime. One mark for a correct account of each side; further marks for making the difference explicit (not two separate definitions).

items.stem: Describe the research methods you would use to answer "How have birth and death rates in Bangladesh changed since 1975, and what explains the fall in fertility?", naming specific sources and explaining why each is appropriate.
items.answer: Download World Bank data (1975–2023); draw line graphs of birth and death rates; calculate natural increase; read two case studies on family planning and girls' education; evaluate data and sources.
items.markingKey: Indicative plan: Download World Bank data (1975–2023); draw line graphs of birth and death rates; calculate natural increase; read two case studies on family planning and girls' education; evaluate data and sources. items.stem: Maya writes: "If birth rates fall below replacement level, the population falls immediately." Explain why this is inaccurate.
items.answer: Because of population momentum and migration, populations can keep growing for years after fertility falls below 2.1.
items.markingKey: Because of population momentum and migration, populations can keep growing for years after fertility falls below 2.1. 1 mark for identifying the error, 1-2 marks for the correct explanation.

items.stem: Give one argument for and one argument against this view: "Rapid population growth is the main cause of poverty in low-income countries."
items.answer: Disagree: rapid growth can make development harder, but poverty has many causes and often drives high fertility itself.
items.markingKey: Arguments for: fast growth puts pressure on schools, health care, jobs and land; young dependants reduce savings per person. Arguments against: poverty often causes high birth rates rather than the reverse; governance, conflict, trade and history are major causes of poverty. Supported judgement: Disagree: rapid growth can make development harder, but poverty has many causes and often drives high fertility itself.

items.answer: Natural increase is births minus deaths; total population growth also includes net migration.
items.markingKey: Natural increase is births minus deaths; total population growth also includes net migration. One mark for a correct account of each side; further marks for making the difference explicit (not two separate definitions).

items.stem: Explain why "How have birth and death rates in Bangladesh changed since 1975, and what explains the fall in fertility?" is a suitable research question for an MYP investigation into population growth: birth rate, death rate and natural increase.

The demographer argued that the number of children in the world has stopped growing: there are about 2 billion children today, and the UN expects about the same number in 2100. World population will still grow because today's children will grow up and live longer, not because more babies are being born.

items.markingKey: Elena: modern cities grow because of connections – transport, trade and links to other places. Hana: site still affects flood risk, water supply and building costs. Judgement (1-2 marks): Situation is usually more important for growth today, while site was more important for a settlement's origin and still affects risk and cost.

items.stem: Write one well-structured paragraph (Point, Evidence, Explanation, Link) in answer to this question: Explain why death rates fell in many countries during the 20th century.
items.answer: Vaccines, antibiotics, clean water and sanitation, better nutrition and health care reduced deaths, especially among infants and children.
items.markingKey: Content: Vaccines, antibiotics, clean water and sanitation, better nutrition and health care reduced deaths, especially among infants and children. Structure: a clear point that answers the question, specific evidence, explanation that links evidence to the point, and a closing link. Criterion C (communicating): appropriate style and register for the purpose, a clear structure suited to the format (topic sentence, developed evidence, explanation, link back to the question), accurate subject terminology, and sources documented with a recognised convention (MLA or APA).

items.stem: Jonas is investigating population distribution and density, and the physical and human factors that affect them and proposes the research question: "Where do people live?" Explain one weakness of this research question and write a more focused alternative.
items.answer: Weakness: it is too broad – it covers the whole world and has no explanatory focus Improved: "Why is the population of Peru concentrated on its narrow coastal desert rather than in the Amazon region?"
items.markingKey: 1 mark: weakness identified (it is too broad – it covers the whole world and has no explanatory focus); 1-2 marks: a focused question such as "Why is the population of Peru concentrated on its narrow coastal desert rather than in the Amazon region?" (clear scope – place, period or group – and open, researchable wording); 1 mark: justification of the change. Criterion B (investigating): a clear, focused research question whose relevance is justified, a realistic action plan, appropriate and varied methods/sources, and reflection on the process.

items.stem: A small town of 2,900 people is the service centre for 5 villages with populations of 2,900, 1,600, 2,700, 1,900, 4,000. The threshold population for a hospital is about 100,000. Calculate the total population of the sphere of influence and state whether the town is likely to support a hospital.
items.answer: 16,000 people – no, below the threshold
items.markingKey: Villages 13,100 + town 2,900 = 16,000 (M1 A1); compared with threshold 100,000 → unlikely to support it (R1).

items.stem: Maya is investigating population growth: birth rate, death rate and natural increase and proposes the research question: "Why are there so many people?" Explain one weakness of this research question and write a more focused alternative.
items.answer: Weakness: it is vague and based on an opinion, with no place or period Improved: "How have birth and death rates in Bangladesh changed since 1975, and what explains the fall in fertility?"
items.markingKey: 1 mark: weakness identified (it is vague and based on an opinion, with no place or period); 1-2 marks: a focused question such as "How have birth and death rates in Bangladesh changed since 1975, and what explains the fall in fertility?" (clear scope – place, period or group – and open, researchable wording); 1 mark: justification of the change. Criterion B (investigating): a clear, focused research question whose relevance is justified, a realistic action plan, appropriate and varied methods/sources, and reflection on the process.

items.stem: 2023 estimates: Nigeria – population 223,800,000, area 923,768 km²; Germany – population 84,500,000, area 357,592 km². Calculate the population density of each country and state how many times more densely populated Nigeria is than Germany.
items.answer: Nigeria: 242.3 /km²; Germany: 236.3 /km²; Nigeria is about 1.0 times as dense.
items.markingKey: M1 density = population ÷ area for each; A1 242.3; A1 236.3; A1 ratio 1.0 (allow ±0.2). A high national density can hide very uneven distribution.

items.stem: Analyse one strength and one limitation of this view: "Situation is more important than site for the growth of a settlement today."
items.answer: Situation is usually more important for growth today, while site was more important for a settlement's origin and still affects risk and cost.
items.markingKey: Arguments for: modern cities grow because of connections – transport, trade and links to other places; technology can overcome most site problems. Arguments against: site still affects flood risk, water supply and building costs; many historic cities owe their origin to site. Supported judgement: Situation is usually more important for growth today, while site was more important for a settlement's origin and still affects risk and cost.

items.stem: Plan an extended response to the question: "Rapid population growth is the main cause of poverty in low-income countries." To what extent do you agree? Give a thesis, two arguments with specific evidence, a counter-argument and a conclusion.
items.answer: Thesis: Disagree: rapid growth can make development harder, but poverty has many causes and often drives high fertility itself.
items.markingKey: Arguments for: fast growth puts pressure on schools, health care, jobs and land; young dependants reduce savings per person. Counter-arguments: poverty often causes high birth rates rather than the reverse; governance, conflict, trade and history are major causes of poverty. Thesis/conclusion: Disagree: rapid growth can make development harder, but poverty has many causes and often drives high fertility itself. Credit a thesis that answers the question, logically ordered paragraphs each with specific evidence, a counter-argument that is weighed, and a conclusion that follows. Criterion C (communicating): appropriate style and register for the purpose, a clear structure suited to the format (topic sentence, developed evidence, explanation, link back to the question), accurate subject terminology, and sources documented with a recognised convention (MLA or APA).

items.stem: Evaluate the claim: "Physical factors are more important than human factors in explaining population distribution."
items.answer: At the global scale physical factors explain the broad pattern, but at regional and local scales human factors are increasingly decisive.
items.markingKey: Arguments for: climate, water and relief set limits – deserts, ice caps and mountains are sparsely populated; most dense areas are fertile lowlands with water. Arguments against: jobs and services in cities draw people regardless of physical conditions, e.g. Dubai; government policy and history shape distribution, e.g. Brasília. Supported judgement: At the global scale physical factors explain the broad pattern, but at regional and local scales human factors are increasingly decisive. Markbands (8 marks): MYP I&S criterion D (year 3), scaled to the marks: 7-8 thoroughly analyses concepts and issues, summarises information to make valid, well-supported arguments, analyses a range of sources in terms of origin and purpose recognising value and limitations, and clearly recognises different perspectives and their implications; 5-6 substantial; 3-4 adequate, partly descriptive; 1-2 limited, mostly assertion.

items.stem:
Source A – Geography textbook (paraphrased): Paraphrase of a standard explanation of the settlement hierarchy in secondary-school geography textbooks, based on Christaller's central place theory (1933)

Settlements can be arranged in a hierarchy. At the bottom are many small hamlets and villages offering few, low-order services. Towards the top are fewer but larger towns and cities offering many services, including high-order ones such as universities, specialist hospitals and international airports.

"Situation is more important than site for the growth of a settlement today." Using Source A and your own knowledge, to what extent do you agree?
items.answer: Situation is usually more important for growth today, while site was more important for a settlement's origin and still affects risk and cost.
items.markingKey: From the source: There are many small settlements with few services and few large ones with many services. Own knowledge for: modern cities grow because of connections – transport, trade and links to other places; technology can overcome most site problems. Own knowledge against: site still affects flood risk, water supply and building costs; many historic cities owe their origin to site. Judgement: Situation is usually more important for growth today, while site was more important for a settlement's origin and still affects risk and cost. Top answers integrate the source with own knowledge and comment on the source's origin/purpose. MYP I&S criterion D (year 3), scaled to the marks: 7-8 thoroughly analyses concepts and issues, summarises information to make valid, well-supported arguments, analyses a range of sources in terms of origin and purpose recognising value and limitations, and clearly recognises different perspectives and their implications; 5-6 substantial; 3-4 adequate, partly descriptive; 1-2 limited, mostly assertion.

items.stem: Which of the following best describes "population density"?
options: Describes an area with few people per square kilometre
The average number of people living in one square kilometre of land
The location of a settlement in relation to its surroundings, such as other towns, routes and resources
The way people are spread out across an area
items.answer: The average number of people living in one square kilometre of land
items.markingKey: B. "population density" is the average number of people living in one square kilometre of land.

items.stem: State what is meant by the term "situation".
items.answer: The location of a settlement in relation to its surroundings, such as other towns, routes and resources
items.markingKey: 1 mark for the core idea: the location of a settlement in relation to its surroundings, such as other towns, routes and resources. Award full marks only if the defining feature is clear; a vague example alone scores 0.

items.stem: Which of the following best describes "death rate"?
options: The main economic or social purpose of a settlement, such as a port, market town or administrative centre
The number of deaths per 1 000 people per year
Describes an area with few people per square kilometre
A feature created by people, such as jobs, transport, services or government policy, that influences where people live
items.answer: The number of deaths per 1 000 people per year
items.markingKey: B. "death rate" is the number of deaths per 1 000 people per year.

items.stem: Distinguish between population density and population distribution.
items.answer: Distribution describes the pattern of where people live; density is a measurement of how many people live per km² in an area.
items.markingKey: Distribution describes the pattern of where people live; density is a measurement of how many people live per km² in an area. One mark for a correct account of each side; further marks for making the difference explicit (not two separate definitions).

items.stem: Distinguish between situation and site.
items.answer: Site is the land a settlement is built on (e.g. a dry hill above a floodplain); situation is its position relative to the wider area (e.g. at the meeting of trade routes).
items.markingKey: Site is the land a settlement is built on (e.g. a dry hill above a floodplain); situation is its position relative to the wider area (e.g. at the meeting of trade routes). One mark for a correct account of each side; further marks for making the difference explicit (not two separate definitions).

items.stem: Explain why educating girls tends to lower birth rates.
items.answer: Educated women tend to marry later, have more job opportunities, know more about family planning and health, and often choose to have fewer children.
items.markingKey: Award marks for: Educated women tend to marry later, have more job opportunities, know more about family planning and health, and often choose to have fewer children. (2 marks: one for each linked point in the chain of reasoning; no marks for assertion without explanation.)

items.stem: Explain why population density alone can be misleading.
items.answer: It is an average over the whole area, so it hides uneven distribution – e.g. Egypt's national density is about 113 per km², but most people are crowded along the Nile.
items.markingKey: Award marks for: It is an average over the whole area, so it hides uneven distribution – e.g. Egypt's national density is about 113 per km², but most people are crowded along the Nile. (2 marks: one for each linked point in the chain of reasoning; no marks for assertion without explanation.)

items.stem: "Site and situation mean the same thing." Explain the flaw in this statement.
items.answer: Site is the local land the settlement is built on; situation is how it relates to its surroundings.
items.markingKey: Site is the local land the settlement is built on; situation is how it relates to its surroundings. 1 mark for identifying the error, 1-2 marks for the correct explanation.

items.stem: "If birth rates fall below replacement level, the population falls immediately." Explain the flaw in this statement.
items.answer: Because of population momentum and migration, populations can keep growing for years after fertility falls below 2.1.
items.markingKey: Because of population momentum and migration, populations can keep growing for years after fertility falls below 2.1. 1 mark for identifying the error, 1-2 marks for the correct explanation.

items.stem: Kenya has about 55,100,000 people (2023) living in 580,367 km². What is its population density?
items.answer: 95 people per km²

items.stem: Which of the following is the most clear and focused research question for an investigation into settlement site, situation and function, and the settlement hierarchy?
options: Why are there so many people?
How does the number and type of services change with settlement size in the district around our school?
items.answer: How does the number and type of services change with settlement size in the district around our school?
items.markingKey: C. It is open, has a clear scope (place/period/group) and can be answered with evidence; the others are too broad, closed or off-topic.

items.stem: In one year the population of a town in Ontario started at 165,000. There were 1,412 births, 1,870 deaths, 4,400 immigrants and 3,000 emigrants. Calculate (a) the natural change, (b) the net migration, (c) the population at the end of the year and (d) state which component contributed more to the change.
items.markingKey: (a) births − deaths = −458 (A1); (b) immigrants − emigrants = +1,400 (A1); (c) 165,000 −458 +1,400 = 165,942 (A1); (d) net migration (larger magnitude) (R1).

items.stem: Sofia argues that "Physical factors are more important than human factors in explaining population distribution." Nia disagrees. Explain one piece of evidence each student could use, and state which view you find more convincing and why.
items.answer: At the global scale physical factors explain the broad pattern, but at regional and local scales human factors are increasingly decisive.

Nia: jobs and services in cities draw people regardless of physical conditions, e.g. Dubai. Judgement (1-2 marks): At the global scale physical factors explain the broad pattern, but at regional and local scales human factors are increasingly decisive.

Source A – Geography textbook (paraphrased): Paraphrase of a standard explanation of the settlement hierarchy in secondary-school geography textbooks, based on Christaller's central place theory (1933)

According to Source A, what can we learn about settlement site, situation and function, and the settlement hierarchy? Support your answer with details from the source.
items.answer: There are many small settlements with few services and few large ones with many services.

items.stem: Briefly describe Japan's shrinking population and explain what it reveals about natural decrease.
items.answer: Japan's population peaked at about 128 million around 2008 and has been falling, with a fertility rate of about 1.2–1.3 and more deaths than births each year. Low birth rates and an ageing population mean deaths exceed births.
items.markingKey: Context (Japan's population peaked at about 128 million around 2008 and has been falling, with a fertility rate of about 1.2–1.3 and more deaths than births each year.) – 1 mark for accurate, specific detail. Link: low birth rates and an ageing population mean deaths exceed births. – remaining marks for explicitly connecting the example to natural decrease.

items.stem:
Source A – UN press release (paraphrased): Summary of the United Nations "World Population Prospects 2022" press release

The world's population reached 8 billion on 15 November 2022. It took 12 years to grow from 7 billion to 8 billion, but it is expected to take about 15 years to reach 9 billion, because growth is slowing. More than half of the increase up to 2050 will be concentrated in just eight countries.

Outline the main argument or view that Source A presents, quoting or referring to the source.
items.answer: World population passed 8 billion in 2022, but growth is slowing and is concentrated in a few countries.
items.markingKey: World population passed 8 billion in 2022, but growth is slowing and is concentrated in a few countries. Award 1 mark per relevant point drawn from the source, up to [3]; own knowledge is not credited here. Criterion D: interpreting a source.

items.stem: A class brainstorm on settlement site, situation and function, and the settlement hierarchy produced the question "What is a settlement?" Explain why it needs refining, then suggest an improved research question and justify your change.

Criterion B (investigating): a clear, focused research question whose relevance is justified, a realistic action plan, appropriate and varied methods/sources, and reflection on the process.

items.stem: In one year the population of a region of Kenya started at 47,000. There were 504 births, 365 deaths, 1,400 immigrants and 5,900 emigrants. Calculate (a) the natural change, (b) the net migration, (c) the population at the end of the year and (d) state which component contributed more to the change.
items.markingKey: (a) births − deaths = +139 (A1); (b) immigrants − emigrants = −4,500 (A1); (c) 47,000 +139 −4,500 = 42,639 (A1); (d) net migration (larger magnitude) (R1).
